name: Vera Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying environmental science, so my week is lectures, a field trip to the river catchment on Wednesdays and a lot of reading. I share a cheap flat above a kebab shop with two other students. Four nights a week I stock shelves at the big supermarket on Harlow Road, because there's nothing else part time around here. I use AI for pretty much everything: summarising papers, making flashcards, even debugging the little scripts I write for my data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit overhyped, but it's still a useful tool, and I'd keep using it. I'd tell friends that the people who learn it properly will have an edge. The big problems are climate and housing, not chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not as relaxed as I sound. My loan, the rent and the few jobs around here are the real worry. If AI only does small things then I'm still a poor student with a degree that might not pay much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the supermarket nights, build my skills in data analysis and try for a placement with the council's climate team. I'd keep using AI tools daily and start a small blog about what I find. And I'd apply for every bursary there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit restless. I'm not scared, but I'm always counting pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said four nights of shelf-stacking. How does that fit around study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tiring. Sometimes I do my coursework at three in the morning in the staff room. I protect Wednesday and Friday mornings, and everything else I fit around. Most weeks I manage; some weeks I'm ill and behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the supermarket cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for gig work, like tutoring GCSE science online, which pays better than stacking shelves. I'd ask my tutor about paid research assistant roles. If both failed I'd take the loan, because dropping out isn't an option.

say: I'd say it's **overhyped** but useful, and people who learn it properly get an edge.
I'd say the real problems are **climate** and housing, not chatbots.
think: Privately, the **loan**, the rent and the lack of nearby jobs worry me more than AI.
A degree that might not **pay** much is the real risk.
do: Keep the **supermarket** nights and try for a placement with the council's climate team.
Apply for every **bursary** and start a small blog about my data work.
S0.quote: Sometimes I do my coursework at three in the morning in the staff room.
fieldNote: Already an **AI** daily user, so the plateau changes little; money is her real pressure.
Practical backup plans: online tutoring and research assistant jobs, and she refuses to drop out whatever happens.

steps.text: Keep the four supermarket night shifts each week
Apply for a placement with the council climate team
Start online science tutoring for school pupils
Use AI tools daily for notes and data scripts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the moment to get ahead. Data cleaning, report writing and mapping go to software, and the people who direct it will be in demand. I'd tell classmates to treat AI like a lab partner, not a rival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a bit scary. The entry-level analyst job I want could be cut, because one person with AI can do what three did. But I know how to work with it, and that's my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a coding minor, build a small portfolio of climate data projects and put it on GitHub. I'd ask my tutor if I can help with a real project. I'd also look for a summer placement in a firm that does environmental assessments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous in equal parts. I like being early on things, but I know the first jobs vanish first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of environmental work do you think software takes over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones who copy-paste AI answers without understanding them. A friend of mine did that all of last term and she can't explain her own report. When jobs thin out, those are the people who get cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your classmates would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also worry about my mum back home, who works in the call centre. Answering customers is exactly what the card says goes first. I'd help her look at courses, and I'd send her money if I could.

say: I'd tell classmates to treat AI like a **lab partner**, not a rival.
I'd say the people who direct it will be in **demand**.
think: Privately, the entry-level analyst job I want could be **cut**, but I know how to work with AI.
I'm excited and **nervous** in equal parts.
do: Add a coding **minor** and put a climate data portfolio on GitHub.
Look for a summer **placement** at a firm doing environmental assessments.
feel: **Excited** and nervous, because first jobs vanish first.
S1.quote: The ones who copy-paste AI answers without understanding them. A friend of mine did that all of last term and she can't explain her own report.
fieldNote: She expects entry-level jobs to **shrink**, but trusts her AI skills as an edge.
Her mother's call-centre job is a real household worry, because answering customers is named on the card.

steps.text: Add a coding minor to the second-year timetable
Build a climate data portfolio and publish it on GitHub
Apply for a summer placement at an environmental firm
Help mum look at courses outside call centres

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and we're not ready, and it's the end of arguing about small things. We need a plan for everyone, because nobody's job is safe. I'd be loud about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd panic a little. By the time I graduate there may be no entry-level jobs left, and my loan won't care. But I'm used to change, so I'd try to ride it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on AI tools, build projects that show I can direct them, and look for any gig that pays now. I'd cut my spending, move back in with my mum for a year if needed, and try to start a small data-consulting side project for local firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, honestly. I'd barely sleep for a week, then I'd settle into a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month after you heard it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum to move her savings, and to learn the AI that does her job before it learns her. She'd say I'm exaggerating, and then she'd ask me to show her. I'd show her that night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also talk to the supermarket manager about full-time hours. If there's going to be a rough patch, I'd want steady wages before the market shifts. It's not glamorous, but it keeps rent paid.

say: I'd say we need a plan for **everyone**, because nobody's job is safe.
think: Privately, I'd **panic** a little, since entry-level jobs may be gone when I graduate.
I'm used to change, so I'd try to **ride** it.
do: Build **projects** that show I can direct AI, and start a data side project for local firms.
Ask for full-time **hours** at the supermarket and cut spending.
feel: **Wired**; no sleep for a week, then a plan.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum to move her savings, and to learn the AI that does her job before it learns her.
fieldNote: She meets the shock with **action** and AI skills, which keeps her anxious rather than alarmed.
Moves quickly to protect rent, mum and income, and does not wait for anyone to give permission.

steps.text: Build AI-directed climate projects for a portfolio
Start a small data-consulting project for local firms
Ask the supermarket for full-time hours
Cut spending and consider moving in with mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who start now. We need to push for retraining and fair rules, but five years is long enough to build something. I'd tell friends to stop complaining and start building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be quite okay. I'd graduate with two years of runway, and I could specialise in something that needs judgement, like environmental policy. It's still scary, but it's the kind I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a data focus, do two placements and build a small consultancy on the side. I'd save a bit every month, and pick up a master's that uses AI. I'd keep the supermarket job only as long as I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly energised. It feels like a race, but one where I know the track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is enough for a degree. What would you do differently from the fast case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's job, and whether the council will still have budgets for climate teams. If public money dries up, those jobs go with it. I'd lobby for green work to be protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also worry about my friends who don't use AI. Some people are more stubborn than scared, and I'd try to drag them along, kindly. Ignoring it won't help anyone, and I'd say that straight.

say: I'd tell friends to stop complaining and **start building**, because five years is enough.
I'd push for retraining and fair **rules** for everyone affected.
think: Privately, I'd be **okay**: I'd graduate with two years of runway and specialise in policy.
It's a race, but one where I know the **track**.
do: Finish with a **data** focus, do two placements and build a small consultancy.
Save every month and do a **master's** that uses AI.
feel: Fairly **energised**; like a race I understand.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build something. I'd tell friends to stop complaining and start building.
fieldNote: Her **energy** comes from familiarity with AI tools; the timeline suits her, and she wants to specialise in policy.
Worries about **public** budgets for climate teams and her mum's call-centre job, and about friends who refuse the tools.

steps.text: Take a data-focused route through the degree
Build a small data consultancy on the side
Save a little from every wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a gift if we use it. I'd say we should invest in people now, in schools, in retraining and in basic income trials. I'd push for that on every platform I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. Ten years means a career: a few jobs, a masters, maybe my own firm. I might even get used to being the person who guides AI on climate projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, do the masters, work for a council or NGO and build my own small practice. I'd keep learning new tools every few months, and I'd save for a flat deposit. I'd also help my mum find something better than the call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite hopeful. A bit giddy, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you want to have built by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to have built a small team that uses AI for flood and heat planning. By 2036 I'd be about twenty-nine and I'd like to be running something real, not just applying to jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everything stays a debate until the last minute. People talk about 2036 like it's a long way off, and then it isn't. I'd rather be ready early and a bit bored than late and scrambling.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if we invest in schools, retraining and basic income trials.
I'd push for that on **every** platform.
think: Privately, I'd feel **good**: ten years means a career, a masters and maybe my own firm.
I'd like to be the person who guides AI on **climate** projects.
do: Study, do the masters, then work for a council or **NGO** and build my own practice.
Save for a **deposit** and help my mum leave the call centre.
S4.quote: I'd rather be ready early and a bit bored than late and scrambling.
fieldNote: The long runway matches her **skills**; she sees a career, not a threat, and plans a small firm of her own.
Wants to bring her mum along, so the hope is **shared**, and she would rather be early than late.

steps.text: Finish the degree and a master's in climate data
Help mum retrain out of the call centre

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd graduate into a market that might not have entry-level jobs, with a loan and a mum who's in the most exposed job there is. What would help is retraining that's actually free, jobs for new graduates protected for a while, and everyone getting a go at the tools. One thing you didn't ask: I'm not scared of AI. I'm scared of people who don't know how to use it getting left behind.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of AI. I'm scared of people who don't know how to use it getting left behind.
portrait: Vera studies **environmental science**, shares a flat above a kebab shop and stacks shelves four nights a week.
She uses AI **daily** for notes, flashcards and little data scripts, and sees it as a lab partner.
Progressive and adaptive, she turns shocks into **projects**, side income and political noise.
Her anchors are the loan and her **mum's** call-centre job, which is the most exposed job in her life.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case worries her most: graduating into no entry-level jobs while her mum's job also goes.
whatWouldHelp: **Free** retraining, some protection for new graduates, and everyone getting access to the tools.
